article_text:
Months after Elon Musk promised that his AI tool Grok Imagine would create an entirely AI-generated, feature-length version of “ The Odyssey ,” the tech mogul has partially followed through on the claim.

On Friday, the company shared the first 7-minute, AI-generated episode of the “Odyssey” series on X . The account also credited the “creative collaboration” to Wonder Studios and director Dev Walker, both of which specialize in AI filmmaking.

Related Stories

Christy Carlson Romano Says Her Salary Was Half of Shia LaBeouf's on 'Even Stevens': 'We Were Co-Leads and Had the Same Screen Time'

In July, Musk announced plans to make a “historically accurate” full-length feature version of Homer’s ancient Greek poem. He noted that his AI “The Odyssey” would be ready by the end of 2026.

Popular on Variety

“Before this year ends, Grok Imagine will make a full-length movie of The Odyssey that is historically accurate and true to the art of Homer,” he wrote, together with an AI-generated 3-minute short of “The Odyssey” posted by an X user.

At the time, “Doctor Strange” and “The Black Phone” director Scott Derrickson pulled no punches and addressed Musk directly on social media to call out the absurdity of the project. “Clearly @elonmusk doesn’t know shit about cinema & he stopped reading in his 20s,” Derrickson wrote on Musk’s social media platform, X. “His opinions on art are worthless.”

While no further statement accompanied the AI-generated episode — or Musk’s original tweet about creating a “historically accurate” version of “The Odyssey” — the move comes after the tech trillionaire repeatedly criticized the film ahead of its release, especially the casting of Elliot Page as Sinon and Lupita Nyong’o as Helen of Troy.

Musk claimed that Nolan cast both actors to satisfy the Academy’s representation and inclusion standards for Oscar eligibility ; in March, he wrote that “Chris Nolan is an anti-White racist,” saying he cast Nyong’o only because “He wants the awards.”

See the first episode of the series here.

article_text:
Filme estreia em 5 de novembro no Brasil.

O Rei dos Monstros está de volta. “ Godzilla Minus Zero ” ganhou seu primeiro trailer internacional completo, continuando a história iniciada com o filme vencedor do Oscar, “Godzilla Minus One”, de Takashi Yamazaki . Assista acima (legendado em inglês).

Foi divulgado também o novo cartaz nacional do filme, abaixo.

Ainda não há confirmação sobre o enredo de “Minus Zero”, apenas que se trata de uma nova ameaça para o povo do Japão após os eventos do primeiro filme. O trailer, no entanto, mostra raios amarelos sendo disparados contra a população, contrastando com o tradicional azul de Godzilla. Com isso, fãs especulam que pode se tratar de King Ghidorah, um dos maiores inimigos do Rei dos Monstros.

O novo filme ainda traz em sua campanha de marketing os dizeres: “Assim que a humanidade conseguiu se agarrar a uma paz duramente conquistada, uma nova ameaça surge, destruindo a esperança num instante. Não haverá uma terceira vez. Tudo termina aqui.” Ou seja, este pode ser o fim desse capítulo de Godzilla nas telonas.

“Minus One” foi um marco para a franquia do Rei dos Monstros. Produzido com um orçamento estimado em apenas US$ 15 milhões, o filme desafiou expectativas e arrecadou mais de US$ 113 milhões em todo o mundo. O longa também se tornou o primeiro na história de 70 anos da franquia Godzilla a ganhar um Oscar, levando para casa a estatueta de Melhores Efeitos Visuais em uma categoria repleta de grandes produções de Hollywood com orçamentos muito maiores. Também se tornou o filme japonês live-action de maior bilheteria de todos os tempos na América do Norte.

“Godzilla Minus Zero” será o 31º longa-metragem japonês da famosa franquia de kaiju (sem incluir as coproduções americanas feitas com a Legendary Entertainment). No Brasil, o filme estreia em 5 de novembro e tem distribuição da Sato Company.

article_text:
O n the floor of the Turbine Hall , there are wide water basins and huge flattish rough-hewn rocks you might see on moorland or in a desert. You can sit or stand or climb on them. But if you look up, you won’t be able to stop looking up – because it’s raining musical instruments. Immense elongated brass trumpets and giant glowing drums seem to float in the air, suspended from the girders of the former power station’s roof.

If Lebanese artist Tarek Atoui had just left it at that, it would be an impressive, intriguing installation, but this is Tate Modern , honey, and Atoui hasn’t been asked to occupy its grandest space with mere physical objects. Instead, his sculptural creations and found stuff resonate and echo with an ever-changing, invisible art of noises. An earth-shaking bass note throbs from a hanging trumpet – or is it from that translucent cone rising out of the ground like an ethereal minaret? Then a drumbeat booms through the space and a woman’s plangent, achingly lovely voice sings notes of infinite nostalgia and melancholy.

It’s entrancing. The music has you hooked. It is music, I think, though abstract, non-melodic, a rising and falling of sounds that lead you around and through the installation’s forest of solid things. But then – is music ever not sculptural? Listening to the scything percussive notes of Stravinsky certainly is; and the desire to crystallise sound waves into something visible has haunted everyone from the inventors of opera to designers of psychedelic lightshows.

Yet Tarek Atoui still manages to do something new and beautiful with sound and vision. He teases you and boggles your mind with how his musical instruments relate to the sounds you hear, how the stones and water basins, pipes and strings have produced this sonic outpouring. The entire installation is an interconnected musical machine.

It’s funny too. There’s a warm, generous if absurdist humour to it all. In the past, a crazy mechanical contraption like this would be called “Heath Robinsonish”, after the early 20th-century British cartoonist who came up with such things. A better comparison is Leonardo da Vinci, who invented wild musical instruments among his other real and impossible machines: organs worked by water, a string instrument shaped like a fantastic beast.

Atoui, like Leonardo, seems to be looking for a lost harmony in the world, a secret note that pleased the Lord. Sadness hovers in the sounds that fill this vast grey space, as the bass notes pound harder, building up to an apocalyptic blast. What is being mourned and where is he taking us? You start to feel you are in a city of sounds and sights. The crowd of towering, floating pinnacles, the mysterious voice and crescendo of percussion, suggest an ancient, tumultuous labyrinth of a city. I thought of Lahore and Marrakesh, of a street-singer heard once in an Istanbul market. Yet this city is purer, less tangible. Its towers fly in the air.

Ultimately, you can’t reduce this magical, elusive work of art to a fixed meaning. You have to surrender to it. The sound gathers you up in its ecstasy like a spiralling mystical dance. There is a strong similarity with Sufi drummers and dervishes who use music and motion to inculcate a liberating, trancelike calm. I certainly didn’t want to leave. The vibrations and complex visual composition keep your brain busy but you are also soothed and at peace.

It also suggests the urban life all around this site, the exotic sounds of Bankside: the music of the city, gathered into Atoui’s collage of random noise. But reality slips and fades as you are shown a world beyond the physical. All these objects, from the cones to the stones to the electric guitar played live at the press view, are but as air. They fascinate the eye but the sound eventually dissolves the material world. The solid stuff Atoui begins with becomes as unreal as a reflection in a courtyard pool.

Atoui has grabbed the opportunity to work in this vast space with both hands, creating something rich, ingenious, funny, sad, mystical. This is a Turbine Hall installation to lose yourself in for hours, dreaming and wondering. It’s the sonic answer to a sun indoors – and Atoui is a modern magus.

article_text:
In an interview conducted earlier this month, after the first large-scale demonstrations in Paris, Jenny Holzer addressed the protests that have continued to roil the city in the weeks since. “It’s gruesome that kids have to fight for a better education or for teachers to be paid properly, for their schools to be clean,” the artist told T: The New York Times Style Magazine . “I worry about the kids’ safety.”

The occasion for the interview was Holzer’s solo show at Musée d’Orsay, which includes an LED panel work that bears a message penned by the French writer Émile Zola in 1860: “I think of the future and see it so dark, so dark that I shrink back terrified.”

A different part of the show features scrolling text projected on the museum’s exterior, including quotations from 30 cultural figures such as Charles Baudelaire, Vincent van Gogh, and Auguste Rodin, and other parts include paintings and sculptures bearing inscriptions, such as a marble bench with a message from artist Mary Cassatt: “As you say the world is mad just now.”

About the quotations she worked with, which came from the archive of the Musée d’Orsay, Holzer told T : “The shock was how contemporary the issues are. And a warm surprise was how companionable the writing is. Sometimes they’re talking about being devastated; other times they’re making bad jokes, pontificating, being vulnerable. It’s like, ‘Oh, hi there. Thank you for passing the time with me.’”

"他向《ARTnews》表示：“这些拍卖都是经过策划、管理，并且为了争取到最好的担保而被推到了极致。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "当拍卖的最后两幅画作——格伦·利贡（Glenn Ligon）的《大银色在演艺界》（Large Silver In Show Business）和比阿特丽斯·米哈兹（Beatriz Hockney）的《狗画17》（Dog Painting 17）登台时，英国人的活力显露无遗。这幅画作首次亮相拍场，引发了掌声以及一场激烈的角逐，佳士得伦敦专家埃德蒙·弗兰西（Edmond Francey）与至少三位通过电话竞标的其他专家参与其中。它最终拍得351万英镑（464万美元）。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "text": "正如第一场拍卖一样，气氛在临近尾声时再度发生了变化。在拍到第27件拍品——最终以150万英镑（198万美元）成交的安迪·沃霍尔的《蒙娜丽莎（反转系列）》（Mona Lisa (Reversal Series)）时，迈耶走下了拍卖台，由王郁歌（Yu Ge Wang）接替主持。随之而来的是一段艰难的胶着期，赛·托姆布莱（Cy Twombly）、乔治·康多（George Condo）、阿尔贝托·贾科梅蒂（Alberto Giacometti）和卢西安·弗洛伊德（Lucian Freud）等人的作品均遭遇流拍。到了晚上8点52分，由擦得发亮的男士乐福鞋和设计师手袋构成的海洋开始逐渐散去。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "就连慈善事业也未能完全盘活全场。伊格沙安·亚当斯（Igshaan Adams）由珠子、线和纺织品制成的雕塑作品《成为一朵玫瑰的笃定（二）》（The certainty of being a rose (ii)）拍得9.6万英镑（12.7万美元），尽管拍卖师提醒竞买人所得收益将捐赠给环保慈善机构。不过，这一结果依然创下了该艺术家的拍卖纪录。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "第二场拍卖按件数计算的成交率为85%，远低于西蒙收藏专场的98%。然而，凭借两件成交价超过2500万英镑的作品，两场合并的业绩让佳士得在11月17日开幕的纽约拍卖之前有充足的理由进行庆祝。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": Christie’s London brought in £218.6 million ($289.4 million) across two evening sales Wednesday, more than doubling last year’s total and offering an encouraging sign for the art market ahead of the New York auctions next month.

Seven auction records were set, including five during the sale of British businessman Peter Simon’s collection, while a Wassily Kandinsky painting fetched £31.6 million ($41.8 million) in the evening’s second auction. (All prices reported include buyer’s premium.) Related Articles At Frieze, an Artist Project in the Fair's Public Toilets Confronts the UK's Ongoing Bathroom Wars Christie's to Sell Barbara Hepworth Sculpture Featured in Vogue Portrait by Lee Miller

The two sales, which coincide with Frieze London and Frieze Masters, achieved a combined sell-through rate of 91 percent by lot and 96 percent by value. The Simon collection, which several market insiders described to ARTnews as the real attraction in London this week, accounted for £107.5 million ($142.3 million) of the total, making it the highest-value single-owner collection ever sold at Christie’s London. The subsequent 20th- and 21st-century sale brought in £111.1 million ($147 million).

There was, however, some confusion about when the festivities were supposed to begin. Although the Simon sale started at 6 p.m., in some places Christie’s live-auction website advertised a 7 p.m. start time. At least three market professionals, including an adviser with a global clientele, had understood that the sale would begin at the later hour. Whether the hiccup caused anyone to miss bidding remains unclear.

Even still, Christie’s was packed when the “Monsoon: The Peter Simon Collection” sale began. Assembled by the founder British retailer Monsoon who has appeared on each edition of ARTnews ’s Top 200 Collectors list since 2005, the collection sold 98 percent by lot and 99 percent by value, with only one of the 41 works failing to find a buyer.

One of the evening’s biggest surprises came from Russian avant-garde painter Liubov Popova, whose Painterly Architectonic sold for £7.64 million ($10.1 million), more than three times its £2.5 million ($3.3 million) high estimate. Setting a new auction record for the artist, the work saw nearly eight minutes of bidding both in the room and on the phones.

Other records set Wednesday came for Bridget Riley’s Streak 2 , which £5.21 million ($6.9 million), and David Bomberg’s San Miguel, Toledo, Afternoon , which brought £3.26 million ($4.32 million). The bidding for the Bomberg work had the room cheering, and the auctioneer even asked for a closer inspection of the painting. Further records were achieved for Portia Zvavahera and Barbara Hepworth.

The Simon collection’s most expensive work, Francis Bacon’s Figure in Movement , fetched £17.19 million ($22.8 million), selling to a bidder in the room, while Piet Mondrian’s Composition A, with Double Line and Yellow brought £9.71 million ($12.86 million). Joan Miró’s Peinture (Les amants – Adam et Eve) sold for £8.56 million ($11.33 million), and Hurvin Anderson’s Last House brought £5.7 million ($7.5 million) against an estimate of £2 million–£3 million ($2.6 million–$3.9 million).

Philip Hoffman, chairman and founder of the Fine Art Group, told ARTnews before the sale that a handful of works in Simon’s collection would race ahead while much of the rest would sell with relatively little competition. Buyers at Frieze Masters, he said, had been holding back money in anticipation of the auction.

Afterward, Hoffman called the two sales a clear indication of a solid market, though he cautioned against reading too much into the totals, especially since 29 of the 41 lots in the Simon evening sale carried third-party guarantees, meaning much of the financial risk had already been accounted for before bidding began.

“These auctions are staged, managed, and already pumped up to the max for the best guarantees they can get,” he told ARTnews .

By the time the auction’s final two paintings, Glenn Ligon’s Large Silver In Show Business and Beatriz Milhazes’s O Rapaz (The Boy) , each sold for £192,000 ($250,000) against low estimates of £400,000 ($529,000) and £300,000 ($397,000), respectively, the room was mute.

In the short break before the 20th/21st Century evening sale, the energy returned, with two Josef Albers works exceeding their estimates, followed by René Magritte’s Le seize septembre , fetching £3.26 million ($4.3 million), well above its £1.8 million ($2.4 million) high estimate.

The zing of the Brits could be felt when David Hockney’s Dog Painting 17 came under the hammer. The painting, appearing at auction for the first time, prompted applause and a spirited contest involving Christie’s London specialist Edmond Francey and at least three other specialists bidding by telephone. It eventually fetched £3.51 million ($4.64 million).

The patriotic spirit continued with British painter Flora Yukhnovich’s Capriccio , which fetched £2.2 million ($2.9 million), against a high estimate of £1.5 million ($1.98 million).

But silence fell over the room for Mondrian’s Composition III (1920), as spectators and bidders alike took out their cameras to record the moment the painting sold for £25.2 million ($33.4 million), squarely in the middle of its £20 million–£30 million ($26.5 million–$39.7 million) estimate.

Though the Mondrian was expected to achieve the highest price going into the auction, Kandinsky’s Das bunte Leben proved to be the bigger attraction. Auctioneer Adrien Meyer described it as “the most important early work by the artist to ever come to auction.” Nearly 20 bids ricocheted across the room, with Christie’s specialists Amelia Walker, Katharine Arnold, and Maria Los competing for the work. Los ultimately secured the painting on a £27 million ($35.7 million) hammer bid, bringing the final price to £31.56 million ($41.79 million), against a £25 million high estimate. The painting had been restituted to the heirs of Hedwig Lewenstein-Weyermann in 2023.

As with the first sale, the mood changed again toward the end of the auction. At the 27th lot, Warhol’s Mona Lisa (Reversal Series) , which ultimately sold for £1.5 million ($1.98 million), Meyer stepped away from the rostrum and Yu Ge Wang took over. What followed was a difficult stretch, with works by Cy Twombly, George Condo, Alberto Giacometti, and Lucian Freud among those failing to find buyers. By 8:52 p.m., the sea of polished loafers and designer handbags had started to disappear.

Even a charitable cause could not entirely revive the room. Igshaan Adams’s The certainty of being a rose (ii) , a sculpture made of beads, thread and textile, fetched £96,000 ($127,000) despite the auctioneer reminding bidders that proceeds would benefit environmental charities. The result nevertheless established an auction record for the artist.

The second sale finished with an 85 percent sell-through rate by lot, well below the Simon collection’s 98 percent. Yet with two works selling for more than £25 million, the combined results gave Christie’s plenty to celebrate ahead of its New York sales, which begin November 17.

For Hoffman, the evening’s results were encouraging but not necessarily conclusive, and the extensive use of guarantees should be taken with a grain of salt. He added that he waiting for the sale of the Antonio Homem Sonnabend collection, estimated to bring more than $50 million and offered without guarantees, for a clearer reading of the market.

⁠Jurandir Filho ⁠, ⁠ Rogério Montanare ⁠, ⁠ Thiago Siqueira ⁠ e ⁠ Fernanda Bermoltz ⁠ conversam sobre como existem filmes e séries que todo mundo acha bons. Existem aqueles que quase todo mundo considera ruins. E existem as obras que simplesmente dividem a humanidade em dois lados: ou você ama, ou você odeia! Neste RapaduraCast, entramos no território das produções mais POLARIZANTES do cinema e da televisão. Aquelas que transformaram qualquer conversa entre amigos em debate, criaram guerras nas redes sociais e que, mesmo anos depois, continuam provocando discussões apaixonadas. Falamos sobre “Batman vs Superman: A Origem da Justiça” , “Star Wars: Os Últimos Jedi” , “Venom”, “Friends” , “Game of Thrones”, “Lost” e muito mais.

Mas por que algumas obras provocam reações tão extremas? O que faz um filme ser considerado uma obra-prima por uns e um desastre completo por outros? Expectativa? Nostalgia? Fandom? Crítica especializada? Ou simplesmente gosto pessoal?

“If you could hear it, you would think I was killing an animal.”

That’s Pedro Pascal on his cello playing, more than a year after he started lessons for a movie that hadn’t been greenlit yet. The star first had lunch with Tony Gilroy in late July 2025 about taking on the lead role of his latest movie, “ Behemoth! .” But even before anything was signed, and before he knew whether the project would hold together, Pascal went straight to cellists Timothy Loo and Charlie Tyler and got to work.

Cameras would eventually roll across Los Angeles at the end of that October, with a final day in Vienna. Every lunch break and short weekend went to “the next thing, and the next thing.” Pascal calls it “a highly intense lip sync” that left him back-footed for the entire shoot, and “the hardest thing that I’ve ever done.”

It was also his favorite filmmaking experience ever. “I miss ‘Behemoth!’ more than I miss anything I’ve ever done,” he tells Variety . “I miss the character.”

We’ve waited a long time for Pascal to play a part like Alex Serian. I suspect a lot of Latinos felt the same.

Pascal, 51, spent two decades in small roles onstage and on television before HBO’s fantasy epic “Game of Thrones” changed his life at 39. He then became the internet’s shared boyfriend through Disney+’s “Star Wars” series “The Mandalorian” and HBO’s post-apocalyptic drama “The Last of Us.” No one gave him a part worthy of what he can do with his face when he has no lines.

Alex, a gifted cellist who comes home to Los Angeles after 20 years on the road, is that part. The Searchlight Pictures film, written and directed by Gilroy, premiered as the centerpiece selection of the New York Film Festival on Oct. 2 and opens Dec. 4. It refuses to reveal what it’s actually about until well past the midpoint.

On this episode of the Variety Awards Circuit Podcast , Pascal digs into Gilroy’s ode to movie composers and a character who says more with a bow than he ever does with words. He also coughs up a line from the upcoming “ Avengers: Doomsday ,” teases his role in Todd Haynes’ anticipated “De Noche” and sends a message to his friend and favorite awards-season foe, Kieran Culkin.

Before that, the return of the Awards Circuit roundtable looks at this season’s Oscars contenders, including whether Nathan Fielder’s “You Can See Everything” is taking on frontrunner status over “The Odyssey.”

Listen below.

The conversation has been edited and condensed for clarity.

I wrote that this is the role I’ve waited a long time for you to play . Thank God Tony Gilroy is alive and well.

He is a spy for the rebellion. Tony kind of blows my mind. He’s so skilled at so many classical elements, classical music being a huge part of this movie and he’s so innovative and progressive in the way he deals with narrative structure while painting completely whole human beings. In my research, and in my love of him now that I’ve gotten to work with him, there’s something I pay even more attention to as I revisit everything he’s written. “Dolores Claiborne,” in 1995, is a manifesto on misogyny. At the time that didn’t feel new, but within the thriller genre, its intelligence around such a real issue left a mark on me. It’s like school in a way. As personal and intimate as this story is, there’s something really rebellious about it and a little anarchistic, in insisting that you pay such close attention to this life puzzle that anyone can have if they want to reflect on their own lives and hear the music of it and let the music guide you into revelations about yourself.

The film doesn’t reveal what it’s really about until maybe 65 or 70% in, and it subverts every expectation of what a drama about classical music could be. You do so much acting with your face. I cried at the end because of a face you make in a pivotal scene. Was it harder to go through this story without a lot of words to show what you’re feeling?

I loved it more than anything I’ve gotten to do. I guess because there are fewer lines to learn. [ laughs ]

There was so much language in the cello playing that speaks for the character. He’s very obviously someone who expresses himself through his music and fails at so many things in life because he doesn’t know how to speak the language of human relationships. He knows how to navigate his own life and express himself through playing the cello. That was something I understood really deeply and had empathy for. I’m somebody who talks a lot and uses a lot of words and loves language, but I related to this untethered, nomadic person whose skill beyond playing the cello is adaptability to survive. That was a deep connection for me.

The homework, beyond the insane technical challenge of looking like I played the cello convincingly, was understanding Tony and the story he was telling. It’s funny, because we recently noticed, while taking the train together, that we’re talking a lot more about Alex Serian than we ever did while shooting the movie.

That happened organically?

Completely organically. Tony puts so much faith in the people he hires, and I think that faith is a form of leadership that invites your most devoted work. He’ll say it’s pragmatic, which I totally understand, because as a leader you want your crew and your cast to give you their best. At the same time, it’s this very warm and exciting invitation to be inside the story without having to talk about it too much. I was given all this permission to step into a day of shooting, into a scene, into pivotal or subtle moments of this very interesting arc the character is on, without talking to Tony about it first. The only time he’d come in and make little adjustments, suggestions even, he would always start with, “I don’t want to fuck with this. But do you think maybe we can put a smile on this?” And he didn’t mean my face. He meant internally, energetically. It was a fascinating dance of trust.

I would say it’s the hardest thing I’ve ever done, because of the cello. But it was also the most nurturing and rewarding experience: playing someone so private, with a camera on him and knowing that everything he doesn’t share with the people orbiting him in the story is being shared with the audience. It’s an interesting kind of present vulnerability that you had to show up for all the time. As recessive as he may feel, the audience is with him. I can’t hide anything from you guys. Anything he doesn’t understand himself, even if he’s looking at something that’s a big reveal and we as an audience aren’t meant to know what he’s seeing, because he doesn’t know how to process what he’s seeing in that moment.

Olivia Wilde slays in this movie. I thought she was going to murder you.

She was my favorite character on the page, and that we got Olivia was, as Tony would say, the movie gods smiling upon us. Coming in and slaying the hell out of the scene.

How much did you see of yourself in Alex? You’re famous, you’re surrounded by people constantly. Did you feel a connection to what it’s like to be lonely?

This is what I find so fascinating, and it’s why I’m talking so much more about him now. I don’t want to use the word “defending” him, but I’m sharing what I understand of him, because I don’t believe he lacks connections or doesn’t know how to connect. What he cannot meet in many of his relationships is a certain expectation of him that goes beyond the realm of a language he knows how to speak. Without it being calculating, he does choose to be in relationships that have their guardrails set in place. Love with a woman who is in a relationship. Nonattachments. Out of his own fear of bringing anyone into his inherited pain and his inherited dysfunction. He’s not somebody to blame his parents. He just is who he is, and he’s doing his best.

The second language he’s very good at is intimacy. Not emotional intimacy, but he can express himself through, I guess, lovemaking. That’s why there are so many relationships in the movie that I feel have very real connections. It just doesn’t come into commitment. There are people who, let’s say, put a demand on him: “I need you to say something, because I’m not willing to say it.” He doesn’t know how to say it, but it isn’t necessarily fair to demand that he be the one to say it.

You had never picked up a cello. Why are you good at everything ?

I’m bad at a lot of things. If you could hear it, you would think I was killing an animal.

You can’t just let the bow slide up and down the strings. It has to be primed to press against the string and attempt to play the note. But to marry all of it, the bowing with the fingering and the different positions and the vibrato, is a lifelong endeavor that lifelong cellists are struggling with to this very day. My teachers suffer at the hands of it even now. So it was a highly, highly, highly intense lipsync, shatteringly difficult and I felt back-footed the entire time.

I had an intensive period before we started shooting. I had lunch with Tony in late July, and we started toward the end of October. Before anything was signed, as soon as I understood there was a green light, whether it would fall apart or not, I didn’t care. I went straight into my lessons with Timothy Loo and Charlie Tyler, these incredible musicians. Then when we started shooting, whatever window we had, whatever lunch, whatever short day, weekend, I was learning the next thing and the next thing and the next thing. It was crazy. The very last day of shooting was in Vienna, but we spent every day of the shoot all over Los Angeles, which had its own magic.

What a concept, to shoot a movie about L.A. in L.A …

So many locations. We were in Pasadena. We were in Studio City. We were in Malibu. We were in the Arts District. We were downtown. Getting to take a break and feel integrated into the city, then go home at the end of the day, was a dream experience. Everyone felt it. The whole crew was local. Damián García, our brilliant cinematographer, lives in Barcelona and our incredible producer Sanne Wohlenberg lives in London, but everyone else, all the department heads, were Los Angeles, if not Angelenos. Major legacy industry people who had worked on the most incredible things. We were all very in love.

Tony told me it would’ve been a lie to make this movie about the business and not shoot it here.

When you talk about Olivia Wilde tearing into the movie the instant she steps on-screen, that’s a perfect example of movie magic we haven’t talked about enough. That scene takes place in Chicago, but we shot it in downtown Los Angeles. It was not cold, and it was not snowing. It is an operatic blizzard happening in this movie. That’s down to our incredible camera department and production design. And Mary Zophres, the costume designer, picked out that emerald green dress for Olivia and worked with me on every detail. What Alex is wearing isn’t necessarily something you notice, but it has everything to do with the gentle nature in which he tries to exist in the world.

The last scene we see of him, in the cathedral, that sweater. He seems so calm, so at peace. And when he’s running through the house, the white shirt and the bow tie, he feels like a man on a mission. As close as we’ll get to you playing James Bond.

The white shirt and bow tie don’t hurt. It’s all so intentional. Everything I wore was this collaborative, gorgeous conversation with Mary. I can’t say enough about everybody who worked on the movie.

You spent about two decades taking small roles onstage and on television before “Game of Thrones” changed everything. You were 39. Someone out there is in those forming years, waiting for that moment. What do you wish someone had told you back then?

I was thinking about a different version of this today, weirdly. One of the first things I got to do when the season was airing was go back to my roots and play Don John in “Much Ado About Nothing” at Shakespeare in the Park, which Jack O’Brien directed. I caught myself thinking about that very, very pivotal year of my life, one I’d been waiting for ever since I left high school and how much I missed it. Then I was thinking about how much I missed shooting “The Last of Us” in Alberta and sharing “The Last of Us” with the world. And then: I miss “Behemoth!” I miss “Behemoth!” more than I miss anything I’ve ever done. I miss the character. I miss being with everyone every day. I miss Tony. And I was thinking, you’re going to look back, so be very present today, because it’s only going to take a couple of years to miss this. Pay attention. Enjoy it.

What I would tell anyone is that if you’re waking up every day and trying, and some days that means not doing anything at all, but you have intention behind your pursuit, you’re in love with what you’re pursuing and you’re pursuing it in your own way, you are exactly where you’re supposed to be. Have faith in that. I think it’s a huge mistake if you feel like you need to mold yourself into something that doesn’t feel true to yourself, or meet an expectation that even fractionally feels like some kind of internal betrayal.

You’ve got to eat shit, and you’ve got to take a lot of shit. That’s part of it. It’s a huge part of it for me, because it forms character, hopefully in the direction of knowing how to treat other people and protecting the value of generosity, because it comes around. There isn’t any way I would be here were it not for the generosity of others who have been there for me. I owe it to all the people in my life. I wouldn’t know where to begin. It’s a population of people that I owe things to.

It makes me think of the finale of “The Office,” when Andy says “I wish there was a way to know you’re in ‘the good old days’, before you’ve actually left them.”

That’s exactly what I was thinking about today.

I was in bed, and I saw the premiere of “Smells Like Teen Spirit” on MTV and I just didn’t blink. “What is this?” I remember the first time I saw Tracy Chapman. I remember the first time I saw Sinéad O’Connor’s “Nothing Compares 2 U” and just being changed.

When I was a kid, I was so into Motown. I was so into classic rock. I had my whole period with Bob Dylan and the Doors and Led Zeppelin and the Rolling Stones. God, Roberta Flack. I walked two miles to get the 1978 self-titled album once I’d heard “The First Time Ever I Saw Your Face.” But through the lens of my nephews, I see how much access the young generation has to express themselves through social media, which has its advantages and its dangers. Major dangers. But it’s also a very important tool of expression, or at least, for older people like us, a way of bearing witness to what their experience is, what their needs are. I’m really excited about young people seeing this movie, even though it’s old farts making it, because there’s something so relatable about evaluating your own life and realizing it has its own music, its own movie. If you follow that music, there are surprises.

You’re famously generous on red carpets and in interviews. When people ask what it’s like to interview you, I say you’re exactly the way you imagine him to be. The internet has turned you into a kind of “shared boyfriend.” Uly Morazan, who’s a content creator and makes videos about you, is a great example of that. Everyone feels they can connect with you. Does that version of Pedro make it harder to disappear into someone like Alex?

Oh my god, I love Uly. It’s not harder for me at all, because I think so dramaturgically about work. That’s my training and the way my brain works. There are so many different types of actors. There are actors who can live in the perspective of their character so completely that I envy them sometimes. There are actors who are writers, even though they don’t write and can save a character and elevate a character through their own contributions of language. There are actors who think producerially and see the whole picture and their place in it. The challenge would come from anyone who sees me in a particular way and hasn’t seen me do something like this. But something like this is a thing I’ve been dreaming about my whole life.

And in its own tiny way, I’ve gotten to play very rich roles in tiny theaters all around the country through my theater career and my years as a member of Labyrinth Theater Company in New York. So the short answer is no. It’s a lot harder to step into Marvel or a beloved video game. You have to be realistic about those expectations and also protect the personal authorship you’re ultimately going to want to share with an audience that’s either new to the project or beloved fans of it. That’s a fascinating balance to understand and study, because you can’t betray anything about yourself. It just won’t be true. You have to accept that you’re not going to meet everybody’s expectations, but you do have to take expectation into account, because these are people who understand the material in a way that’s very important for you to understand when you go into it.

I was told you can tell me almost everything about “Avengers” and the Todd Haynes film. So tell me everything.

You want me to tell you everything about “Doomsday” and “Secret Wars” together? They are about the Avengers and major events that all of us are a part of.

I asked David Harbour, who sat in that very spot, for one line his character says, completely out of context. Give me a line from “Avengers.”

I’m trying not to pick the line that’s in the trailer … “It’s good to see you again.”

And Todd Haynes’ “De Noche?”

“De Noche” has its own movie gods, one of them being Todd Haynes. It’s a sister film for me, emotionally anyway, in terms of how special it is to me. For both of them, there were only these windows for them to be made and to be able to fly in through that window together is its own sort of magic. To me, it was a movie that had to be made, a Todd Haynes movie that had to be made, just like this is a Tony Gilroy movie that had to be made.

Kieran Culkin isn’t in a film this year, and I’m going to miss the banter you both shared during “The Last of Us” and while he was on the circuit for “Succession.” If you had a message for Mr. Culkin, what would it be?

Oh, Kieran … He’s not going to listen to this, so I’ll text it to him.

“ Come here, Kieran. Let’s cuddle. ”

10 QUESTIONS WITH PEDRO PASCAL

What’s your childhood nickname?

“Pepelo.” If I had grown up in Chile, I would be Papelo.

Something you loved as a kid that you can’t believe you were into?

I think I love everything I was into. But I fell for Cabbage Patch Kids, and now I’m like, why?

My father-in-law fell for the Beanie Babies revolution. Thought they’d be worth a gazillion dollars.

That was a craze, though. I moved on to Garbage Pail Kids, and I don’t regret that at all.

Go-to karaoke or shower song?

“La Bamba.” But I don’t do karaoke.

Not even at a friend’s house?

I’ve done “La Bamba” for friends.

So I just need to get invited. Secret talent?

I have few secrets and very, very few talents. I used to know how to juggle. Can’t juggle anymore. Just tried. Big mistake. I’m good at laundry.

You fold well?

Fold well.

Favorite ice cream flavor?

Chocolate Häagen-Dazs. Without question.

Mine is cookies and cream Häagen-Dazs.

That’s my second, bro. If it’s not chocolate, the closest second is cookies and cream Häagen-Dazs.

The one item you can’t live without?

Something my mother made me.

What TV show or film in history do you wish you’d been a cast member of?

I wish I was in “The Lost Boys.” Can I also say “Twin Peaks?”

Did you see “The Lost Boys” musical?

No, but I heard it’s amazing. Michael Arden is a friend of mine. We worked together on “King Lear,” and he’s an incredible director.

Fictional character you most relate to or admire?

Did you ever see “My Life as a Dog?” Ingemar, in Lasse Hallström’s movie.

I had chills for a second, because my answer to that is usually “My Life,” with Michael Keaton and Nicole Kidman. Nobody talks about that movie. I think it’s Keaton’s finest hour. Favorite piece of advice, given or received?

It’s corny as hell, and it’s a verse from Shakespeare. But to thine own self be true.

ゲッティイメージズ、米破産法11条の適用申請へ。競合との大規模統合を断念、再建目指す

アメリカ の画像・動画ライセンスビジネス大手で、世界各国でサービスを提供する ゲッティイメージズ が、米連邦破産法第11条の適用を申請することを10月12日に発表した。背景には、競合企業との大型事業統合計画の中止がある。

3億点を超える画像・動画などの素材を保有する大手ライセンスビジネス企業、 ゲッティイメージズ が、日本の民事再生法にあたる米連邦破産法第11条（チャプター11）適用を申請すると発表した。同社は、著名実業家チャールズ・コッホ（コーク）が率いるコングロマリットの投資部門による支援を受け、非公開企業として再建を目指すとザ・ハリウッド・リポーター誌（THR）が 伝えている （*1）。

*1 US版ARTnewsとザ・ハリウッド・リポーターはいずれも、2022年秋からゲッティイメージズと世界的な独占メディアパートナーシップを結んでいるペンスキー・メディア・コーポレーションの傘下に属している。

10月12日の発表の背景には、ゲッティイメージズの競合である画像・動画ライセンスビジネス大手、シャッターストックとの37億ドル（約5800億円）規模の事業統合が不調に終わったことがある。2025年1月に公表された統合の目的は、「対等な立場での統合を通じて業界屈指のビジュアルコンテンツ企業を創出すること」とされていた。新会社の社名はゲッティ・イメージズ・ホールディングスで、ゲッティイメージズの最高経営責任者（CEO）であるクレイグ・ピーターズが、そのまま新会社のCEOとなる予定だった。

統合が取りやめになった大きな理由は、 イギリス の競争・市場庁の出した規制条件だった。当局はシャッターストックのエディトリアル部門の売却を求めたが、ゲッティ側はこれを「受け入れ不可能」と判断。THRの報道によると、ピーターズCEOは8月の業績発表で、不成立に終わったシャッターストックとの統合に1億ドル（約158億円）以上が費やされたことを明かしている。

ゲッティイメージズは、2018年から同社を支援してきたコッホ・エクイティ・デベロップメント（Koch Equity Development）から約5億ドル（約790億円）の資金提供を受け、今後数カ月のうちに公開企業から非公開企業へ移行する。ゲッティイメージズの広報担当者はTHRの取材に対し、破産手続きに伴う人員削減は行われず、同社の事業、コンテンツパートナー、および取引先にも影響はないと回答した。（翻訳：石井佳子）

article_text:
Jordan Firstman is bringing “ Club Kid ” to the club.

A24 is set to hold free screenings of Firstman’s feature film directorial debut “Club Kid” for nightlife communities in 12 U.S. cities, including Atlanta , Austin , Boston , Chicago , Dallas , Houston , Miami , Philadelphia , Portland , San Francisco , Seattle and Washington D.C.

The activation is in partnership with Resident Advisor, a global online platform about electronic music, DJs and club scenes.

Related Stories

Japan IP Market to Return to Cannes in 2027 as Tokyo Partnership Continues

The screenings will take place the week of Oct. 26 at around 7 p.m., leaving plenty of time for the kids to get to their clubs that night.

“Club Kid” stars Firstman, who also wrote the screenplay, as a New York City nightlife promoter whose world is turned upside down when he discovers he’s the father of a 10-year-old boy (Reggie Absolom). The cast also includes Diego Calva, Cara Delevingne, Paris Petitjen, Coleen Camp, Kirby-Howell Baptiste, Vicki Pepperdine, Nigil Whyte, Eldar Isgandarov, Saturn Risin9, Miss Benny and Alaska Riley.

After earning a six-minute standing ovation at its Cannes Film Festival premiere in May, “Club Kid” was bought by A24 for $17 million after a heated bidding war with Mubi, Focus Features, Searchlight, A24 and Netflix. Warner Bros.’s new indie label Clockwork and Neon were also early suitors.

“It’s really been the best week of my life,” Firstman told Variety ’s Matt Donnelly shortly after the A24 deal was signed. “It’s been beautiful seeing my mom here, my non-binary sibling who lives a very different kind of queer lifestyle. Watching people fall in love with Diego Calva. I saw a few posts [about me] saying, “Oh God, this is going to make him such a monster.” But I feel the opposite of that. I don’t want to gloat. I’m just so grateful.”

Figures Collection The Body as Ledger

A photographic accounting of neurological episodes that cannot be written off (2012–present).

Figures Collection: The Body as Ledger is an archival practice that registers neurological events through a grammar of transaction rather than testimony. Where expressive disclosure would risk social erasure—reducing the subject to spectacle or pathology—this series adopts the forensic logic of bookkeeping. The body, here, is neither a site of display nor a vessel of narrative, but an instrument of record.

Each photograph captures a single, non-public episode as a figure of constrained physical notation. The form is shaped not by emotion but by the bureaucratic architecture that encloses lived experience: redacted medical reports, contradictory witness statements, formally denied insurance claims. These documents constitute the clinical and administrative perimeter around an event—acknowledging its occurrence while systematically refusing its social or material validation.

The work exists in the liminal space between registration and recognition. It leverages the aesthetics of evidentiary filing, forensic taxonomy, and archival classification to trace how pain is absorbed into systems of documentation, processed into data, and filed as an unsettled account. The transaction is logged but never completed; the entry is made but never closed. The body, in this calculus, is a ledger where pain is accounted for—yet never written off.

article_text:
Sales company The Playmaker Munich has closed further territory deals on animated family adventure film “Pirate Mo and the Legend of the Red Ruby” ahead of the American Film Market, where it will have its market premiere. The film has now sold to more than 50 countries. Variety is debuting the teaser (below).

The latest buyers for the film, helmed by “The Amazing Maurice” co-director Florian Westermann, include Umbrella Entertainment, who took rights for Australia and New Zealand, Israel’s FilmHouse and Vietnam’s Skyline Media.

Spotify Has Removed 50 Million AI Slop Tracks From Recommendations This Year

Previously announced sales include for the Baltics (Garsu Pasaulio Irasai), Benelux (Just4Kids), Bulgaria (Pro Films), Czech Republic and Slovakia (DonArt Production), Ex-Yugoslavia (Blitz), Greece (Rosebud.21), Hungary and Romania (ADS), Middle East (Grand Entertainment for Motion Pictures), Poland (M2 Films), Portugal (Outsider Films), Scandinavia (Njutafilms), Turkey (Filmarti), Ukraine (Svoekino) and North America (Viva Pictures Distribution).

The distributor in Germany and Austria is DCM Distribution, with the theatrical release set for April 29, 2027.

The screenplay for the film, which is based on Kirsten Boie’s novel “Seeräubermoses,” is written by Richie Conroy and Westermann.

The film is set on board a pirate ship, on which a child, Mo, lives with a crew of ragtag seadogs and the ship’s pet … a goat.

Mo, who arrived by chance among the pirates as an infant, has been brought up by the ship’s kindly captain, Claas. One day, she is captured by the wicked pirate Peg Leg Olle, and meets the resourceful cabin boy, Hannes, and his pet bird. Together with Hannes, Claas, his motley crew and their pets, Mo will have to defeat Peg Leg Olle and fulfill her childhood prophecy of finding the Blood Red Ruby of Doom to restore peace and harmony to the land.

The film is produced by Ulysses Films, Letterbox Filmproduktion, Isla Molona AIE, Arxlight Pictures and Arx Anima. The producers are Emely Christians, Sonja Matthes, Michael Lehmann, Holger Ellermann, Dunja Bernatzky, Kris Staber, Nicolás Matji and Edmon Roch.

It is supported by ICAA, OEFI+, DFFF, MOIN Film Fund Hamburg Schleswig-Holstein, FFA, BKM, OEFI, ICEC, FFW and Creative Europe MEDIA Slate Funding.

“Omi,” which will premiere at the Austin Film Festival on Oct. 30, features Bunny Levine in her final film appearance.

Levine died on Aug. 20 at her home in Tarzana, California at the age of 97.

“Omi,” a Jewish exorcism comedy, also marks the directorial feature debut for Emily Lerer. Adam Lebowitz-Lockard wrote and stars in the film alongside Dree Hemingway.

Tuesday Oct. 27

‘Fair Play: The Jordan Chiles Story’ Documentary Set by Campfire Studios and Select Entertainment Andscape announced Tuesday that production has begun on “Fair Play: The Jordan Chiles Story,” a documentary feature about gymnast and Olympic medalist Jordan Chiles. Directed by Trishtan Williams, the film will be released on Hulu and Hulu on Disney+ in the fall of 2027, ahead of the 2028 Olympic Games in Los Angeles.

The official logline for the documentary reads: “Bold, joyful, resilient, and unapologetically herself, Chiles has become one of the most recognizable figures in gymnastics and a powerful voice for a new generation of athletes. The film goes beyond the headlines to reveal the woman behind the performances, capturing Chiles at a pivotal moment in her life as she looks toward what comes next, both inside and outside the gym.”

“My journey in gymnastics has taught me a lot about resilience, perseverance, and the importance of defining success on my own terms,” Chiles said in a statement. “As I work toward LA28, I’m excited to partner with Andscape and Hulu to share more of my story, reflect on the experiences that have shaped me, and explore what it means to step into this next chapter while reclaiming my narrative.”

Monday, Oct. 26

AFI Fest Announces Grand Jury Award Winners

The American Film Institute announced its Grand Jury Prize winners and Special Mentions for the 40th edition of the festival, which ran Oct. 21-25 in Los Angeles.

“Free Eliza (Notes On An Anatomical Imperfection)” from Alexandra Matheou won the prize for best live action short film. Stephen P. Neary’s “Living With a Visionary” was awarded Best Animated Short Film. “A Woman’s Place is Everywhere” from Fanny Texier was selected as the prizewinner for documentary short film.

The Special Jury Mentions for live action shorts include “The Bovine Comedy” by Ratchapoom Boonbunchachoke for Audacity of Vision, “A Breach Within” by Jean-François Leblanc for Cinematography, “Nobody Said Anything” by Tamara Todorović for Screenwriting and “Mutrion” by Marco Cavazzin for Uniqueness of Expression.

The Special Jury Mentions for animated shorts included “Emulsion” by Shiyu (Shino) Tang for Craft, “Trading Cards” by Radheya Jang for Story, “The End” by Niki Lindroth von Bahr for Direction and “Saba” by Liron Topaz for World Building.

The Special Jury Mentions for documentary shorts include “Listen” by Taliesin Black-Brown for Craft, “Water Cooler” by Emma V.F. for Social Impact, “Buckskin” by Mars Verrone for Storytelling and “A Wolf in the Suburbs” by Amélie Hardy for World Building.

The Grand Jury Prize winners for live action, documentary and animated shorts are eligible for Academy Award consideration.

article_text:
This October, Aperture releases Alex Webb: Walking Blues .

In Walking Blues , the acclaimed street photographer Alex Webb traverses some forty cities across the United States, documenting moments of connection between communities with his signature eye for bold color and rhythm. Webb was inspired by the lift and pull of blues music, a quintessential American musical form that scores the nation’s culture, and his photographs express the improvisation of chance encounters. The culmination of more than a decade of intuitive, open-minded exploration, Webb’s latest book is a vivid chronicle of urban life today.

A related installation of prints from Walking Blues will be on view at Aperture at 380 Columbus Avenue from November 18, 2026 through January 10, 2027.

To celebrate the launch, a conversation between Alex Webb and Rebecca Norris Webb will be held on Tuesday, December 8 at 6:30 p.m. EDT at the MFA Photography, Video, and Related Media Department at the School of Visual Arts. Details are available at aperture.org/events.

A limited-edition set will also be available exclusively through Aperture, pairing a deluxe edition of Walking Blues with Philadelphia, PA (2025), a signed and numbered 8 x 10-in. print of the photograph that appears on the back of the book cover. Pricing and details are listed at www.aperture.org.

Alex Webb (born in San Francisco, 1952) has published more than fifteen books, including a survey of his color work, The Suffering of Light (Aperture, 2011); Memory City (2014, with Rebecca Norris Webb); and La Calle: Photographs from Mexico (Aperture, 2016). Webb became a full member of Magnum Photos in 1979. His work has been shown widely, and he has received numerous awards, including a Guggenheim Fellowship in 2007.

News

Art Basel Paris to Close Two Days Early, Citing Protests

Amid ongoing nationwide demonstrations for better living conditions in France, the fair said it will shutter over the weekend “in the interest of safeguarding our visitors.”

Art Basel Paris will prematurely end on Friday, October 23, at 7 pm, “in light of potential demonstrations across Paris this weekend and in the interest of safeguarding our visitors,” event organizers told exhibitors in an email reviewed by Hyperallergic .

The main program of Art Basel Paris was scheduled to run through Sunday, October 25, at the Grand Palais. Following a temporary lockdown during installation on October 17, event organizers proceeded with the original program before announcing the fair's early closure, citing the ongoing nationwide protests over France's failing education system and public services.

French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has stated that military forces from Operation Sentinelle, rather than police officers, will be deployed over the weekend to control protesters. Operation Sentinelle was started in the aftermath of the Charlie Hebdo and Hyper Cacher attacks of January 2015 with a stated aim of defending against terrorism.

"We strongly encourage galleries to keep their representations intact through the fair's close tomorrow at 7 pm, and ask that general move-out not begin until access and removal instructions have been issued," Vincenzo de Bellis, Art Basel’s chief artistic officer, and Karim Crippa, the Paris fair’s director, said in the email to exhibitors.

A gallerist, who asked to remain anonymous, confirmed to Hyperallergic that operations and dismantling instructions are still pending.

Several artist advocacy groups and labor unions, including the Syndicat National des Artistes Plasticiennes, which represents visual artists and graphic designers, had pledged to join a protest outside the fair on Saturday at 4 pm. A flyer for the protest circulating online denounces the “privatization of culture and a market-driven art that accompanies the extreme right-wing shift in our country.”

Artists and organizations elsewhere have also expressed that their artworks will be taken down or prematurely dismantled. Fondation Louis Vuitton will close on Saturday, October 4, according to a banner on their website. Alicja Kwade, who is one of eight artists participating in the public program outside the Grand Palais for the fair's run, took to Instagram to announce the removal of her 14-foot sculpture, "L'Élévation des Mondes"(2026), citing “announced riots and people who simply want to resort to violence.”

The ongoing protests have seen a spate of police brutality against student demonstrators, including a 14-year-old child who was maimed by a tear gas grenade and a 15-year-old whose hand was blown off by a stun gun . Ahead of the protests, French authorities have also enforced strict curfews .

I n the last half-decade Stanley Tucci has been a source of near-inexhaustible on- screen delight, whether making friends with nonnas in his delightful cooking shows or smartly judged supporting turns in Conclave and The Devil Wears Prada 2 . He is an actor well placed for a star vehicle of his own, and this one, Masterplan , sounds good on paper: an art heist fronted by the actor at his most debonair, flanked by a grandson of a French New Wave legend (Victor Belmondo, related to Breathless star Jean-Paul) and a buzzy breakout of The White Lotus (Simona Tabasco, winning in season two of Mike White’s comedy).

There’s a good bit of pulpy fun to have here, with double, triple and quadruple crossing, silly spy gadgetry which has been updated to include retina scan cloning and something called “VR intrusion”. As British criminal mastermind Roger, Tucci is game to send up aristo archetypes, even if his character often veers into parody. “I’m English,” his character says at one point. “‘Not bad’ is what I say when I orgasm.”

“Not bad” is what I say about Masterplan, a straight-to-streaming Amazon Prime offering that the studio is burying this weekend, seemingly choosing to focus on its just-released romantic drama Love of Your Life . Cybersecurity hacker Chiara (Tabasco) and explosives expert Jay (Belmondo) are Europe’s leading young criminals, working together remotely under aliases and using some kind of dark web app to sign up for new gigs. When they meet for the first time while breaking into a mansion on the shores of Italy’s Lake Geneva, sparks fly. “Sixty seconds, in and out,” promises Jay before Chiara snaps back playfully: “Don’t you use that name on Tinder?”

Just as you settle in for an evening of will-they-won’t-they hijinks, the film pulls a bait and switch. It turns out that the pair have been set up by Roger (Tucci), a veteran thief himself who has the “job of a lifetime” for them: a decade-in-the-making plan to make off with the Mona Lisa in a complicated scheme that involves drones, trickery, truffle-related espionage and a long-forgotten tunnel that conveniently exists under the Louvre. Also: they are in fact brother and sister, the result of an energetic mid-90s for Roger when he seduced their respective mothers.

You would think the fact that they are now siblings would put the kibosh on Jay and Chiara’s flirtation, but the film seems to feel otherwise. As the makeshift family relocate to Paris to put plans in motion for the heist, Chiara makes jokes about the size of her half-brother’s “hammer” and offers to settle squabbles through a round of strip poker, which strikes me as an unusual way for siblings to bond.

Despite the jokes that land with a thud, Masterplan is on safer ground when it sticks to the espionage. That is thanks to Thomas Vincent, the director, recapturing some of the juice he showed in the episodes of Bodyguard he directed, and I would rate Masterplan as a hair better than Role Play , the dull film he previously made for Amazon. When it isn’t trying to dazzle you with technology, Masterplan has a few twists on heist movie tropes (including a very clever use of a helium balloon) that avoids it feeling like a total retread of the Ocean’s 11 franchise, even if it doesn’t come close to matching the ingenuity of those films. And while the characters are too thinly drawn to make you care too much about them, I appreciated flourishes that nod to the female and gay male gaze, such as the diva moment where Tabasco’s character dons a platinum blond wig and the camera’s lustiness for Belmondo, who has a talent for losing his shirt.

Everything isn’t as it seems, and while the film should really end 30 minutes before it does, it has a few final tricks up its sleeve in the third act, as the characters begin to learn who they can really trust and Chiara’s hacking skills are put to the test once more. Even as the plot becomes increasingly ridiculous, ample bangs and explosions ensure that the nearly two-hour runtime doesn’t totally drag. The best you can offer Masterplan is faint praise: it could breeze by as company to your Sunday night takeout even if you will struggle to remember it a week later.
